newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - May 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - May 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BROWN PLANS 10p TAX IN BUDGET

Gordon Brown plans to announce the introduction of a 10p starting rate of income tax in the Budget next month, rather than restrict his initial Budget to issues such as the windfall tax and reducing VAT on fuel. He sees the introduction of the rate as an essential part of the welfare-to-work programme. The date of the Budget is yet to be announced, but 10 June is thought likely.
-- BT WINDFALL ANGER

British Telecom reacted angrily to a suggestion in an interview in The Observer newspaper with Gordon Brown that it should be subject to the planned windfall tax on privatised utilities. The company said it was not a monopoly but a company with 250 competitors.
-- INTERFLORA REBELS UPROOT DIRECTORS

Florists yesterday voted to remove all 12 directors of Interflora in protest against proposed changes to the structure of the flower delivery company. They voted for the appointment of six new directors to the Interflora board. Another vote will be taken within the next two weeks, with all 2,700 Interflora members balloted by post.
THE TIMES
-- POUND FACES PRESSURE AS BANK STEERS AWAY FROM HIGHER RATES

The pound is likely to come under further pressure this week after Bank of England Governor Eddie George hinted he was satisfied with last week's quarter-point rise in base rates. The Bank is to issue its quarterly inflation bulletin tomorrow and is expected to say there is no need to raise rates further.
-- LABOUR READY TO SHAKE UP JOBLESS COUNT

The Government is to launch a review of unemployment figures, which could change the way they are compiled and calculated. The review is intended to restore credibility to key figures, widely regarded as compromised. The latest unemployment figures, to be announced Wednesday, are expected to show a further fall from their current level of 1.7 million.
-- SIR ROCCO SET TO CHECK IN AS CHIEF OF TORY COFFERS

Sir Rocco Forte is likely to take on the role of Treasurer of the Conservative Party after its expensive election defeat. He is likely to take over the role from Lord Hambro, chairman of Hambros Bank, at present caught up in the scandal over the failed takeover of the Co-operative Wholesale Society.
THE GUARDIAN
-- HIGH NOON FOR PENSION FIRMS

The largest pensions companies and their City regulators have been called to meetings at the Treasury on Wednesday to solve the problems delaying compensation to the 600,000 victims of the pensions mis-selling scandal. The move reflects the determination of Helen Liddell, the new City minister, to conclude the saga.
-- BROWN TANTALISES EU LEADERS

Chancellor Gordon Brown will today brief European commissioners on how the government intends handling relations with the planned single European currency. The move follows speculation that the pound may rejoin the exchange rate mechanism during Britain's presidency in the first half of next year.
-- CRS WANTS TO LEARN FROM SISTER

Co-operative Retail Services chairman Peter Rowbotham revealed at the weekend that the company is seeking protection against the type of hostile bid that recently threatened its sister organisation, Co-operative Wholesale Society. The chairman said commercial success remained the best defence, but that legal means were also being sought to strengthen co-operatives.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BECKETT RULES OUT MOVE TO SELL POST OFFICE

Board of Trade President Margaret Beckett yesterday ruled out any moves by the government to privatise the Post Office, but backed its call for more commercial freedom. She said privatisation was not in the public interest, but discussions on freeing up the organisation are likely to be held in the near future.
-- STEEL MAKERS OPPOSE EU TAX

Heavy industrial energy users last night warned Chancellor Gordon Brown to veto plans by the European Commission to impose a carbon tax on member states. They said the proposal would hit jobs and competitiveness. Any new tax requires unanimous support from all member states to become law.
-- BOOK SALES HIT AS CONSUMERS TURN OVER NEW LEAF

A study released today shows that the major supermarket chains' book sales have reached 100 million pounds stg per year, heavily affecting High Street bookshops. Although the chains are restricted to best-sellers and childrens' books, they have taken around 6 percent of the market and are expected to reach double figures soon.
